Whenever we multiply a matrix $A$ by the $n$th column of the identity matrix, the result is the $n$th column of $A.$ For example, consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The first column of the identity matrix $I_2$ is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ If we multiply $A$ by the column on the *right*, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ The product is just the first column of the matrix $A.$ Using the same method, you can check for yourself that when we multiply $A$ by the second column of $I_2,$ the result is the second column of $A.$ On the other hand, if we multiply $A$ by the first *row* of the identity matrix $I_2$ on the *left*, we will obtain the first row of $A$. Indeed, $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & (-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$

Whenever we multiply a matrix $A$ by the $n$th column of the identity matrix, the result is the $n$th column of $A.$ For example, consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The first column of the identity matrix $I_2$ is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ If we multiply $A$ by the column on the *right*, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{3}} & -1 \\ {\color{blue}{1}} & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{3}} \\ {\color{blue}{1}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ The product is just the first column of the matrix $A.$ Using the same method, you can check for yourself that when we multiply $A$ by the second column of $I_2,$ the result is the second column of $A.$ On the other hand, if we multiply $A$ by the first *row* of the identity matrix $I_2$ on the *left*, we will obtain the first row of $A$. Indeed, $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{3}} & {\color{blue}{-1}} \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & (-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{3}} & {\color{blue}{-1}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$
